section_summary: This section covers Japanese zinc smelting and the expansion of Japan’s iron and steel industry, especially its dependence on imported ore and American scrap. It includes statistical memoranda, correspondence about scrap exports, and 1939 records concerning a proposed move of steel machinery from Wooster, Ohio, to Japan and possible steel sales on credit. The final document in this section ends on page 80.

subfiles.title: Document file note on Yawata Steel Works
subfiles.about: Cross-reference to a telegram on government investment in Yawata and industry losses.
subfiles.summary: References telegram 107 and notes roughly 140 million yen invested in Yawata Steel Works.

subfiles.title: Document file note on Steel Merger Law
subfiles.about: Cross-reference to a despatch on consolidation of public and private steel mills.
subfiles.summary: References despatch 348 on the Steel Merger Law.

subfiles.title: Document file note on proposed steel merger
subfiles.about: Cross-reference to criticism of the proposed Japan Iron Manufacturing Company.
subfiles.summary: Notes press and Diet criticism of the planned merger.

subfiles.title: Document file note on zinc smelting
subfiles.about: Cross-reference to a report on sulphur fumes from zinc smelting.
subfiles.summary: Points to despatch 1022 on controlling zinc smelter fumes.

subfiles.title: Zinc Smelting Industry of Japan
subfiles.from: American Consulate General, Tokyo; prepared by Charles A. Hutchinson and approved by Arthur Garrels
subfiles.about: Reports zinc production, smelter locations, fume controls and liability for damage.
subfiles.summary: The report identifies four Japanese zinc smelters and gives production and import figures for 1931–1933. It describes sulphur gas controls, the limited reported damage to nearby property, and potential remedies under mining law or the Civil Code. Tables list zinc output and individual smelter production.

subfiles.title: Iron ore supply and imports in Japan
subfiles.about: Summarizes Japan’s dependence on imported iron ore and its principal supply areas.
subfiles.summary: Tables compare domestic output and imports, including shipments from China and the Straits Settlements.

subfiles.title: Statistics of the Japanese Iron and Steel Industry, With Special Relation to Scrap Iron and Steel
subfiles.from: Office of the Adviser on International Economic Affairs
subfiles.about: Compiles production, trade, reserve and projected requirement statistics for Japan’s iron and steel industry.
subfiles.summary: Tables trace iron ore, pig iron, scrap, ingots and steel products through the mid-1930s and compare Japanese imports with U.S. exports. They also estimate Pacific iron ore reserves and Japan’s 1941 requirements. The memorandum highlights Japan’s growing reliance on imported materials and substantial U.S. scrap shipments in 1937.

subfiles.title: Relation of Scrap Iron and Steel to Development of the Japanese Iron and Steel Industry
subfiles.from: Office of the Adviser on International Economic Affairs
subfiles.about: Analyzes how foreign scrap supplies affect Japan’s steel expansion and wartime production.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum describes rapid Japanese steel expansion and continuing dependence on foreign ore and scrap. It surveys prospective ore sources around the Pacific and explains the sharp rise in American scrap shipments during 1937. It concludes that losing U.S. scrap alone would cause difficulties but would probably lead Japan to seek other materials and restrict civilian steel use.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting iron and steel memoranda to Senator Thomas
subfiles.about: Sends memoranda for a Senate subcommittee studying bills affecting scrap exports.
subfiles.summary: Hull encloses memoranda prepared in Dr. Feis’s office for Thomas’s subcommittee.

subfiles.title: Statistics of the Japanese Iron and Steel Industry, With Special Relation to Scrap Iron and Steel
subfiles.from: Office of the Adviser on International Economic Affairs
subfiles.about: Provides a copy of the statistical memorandum enclosed with Hull’s letter.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats tables on Japanese iron and steel output, imports, ore reserves, projected needs and U.S. shipments. The figures document rising demand for ore and scrap and the U.S. share of Japanese purchases.

subfiles.title: Thomas’s acknowledgment to Hull
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of confidential information about scrap iron and steel.
subfiles.summary: Thomas thanks Hull and promises to keep the memorandum confidential.

subfiles.title: Proposed sale and shipment to Japan of a steel machine plant at Wooster, Ohio
subfiles.about: Records a discussion with businessmen proposing to transfer a Wooster machinery plant to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Arensberg and associates describe a proposed Japanese majority venture funded by machinery supplied for stock rather than cash. Hornbeck says no law bars the transfer and the Department cannot veto it, but explains that the government discourages credit transactions with Japan. The businessmen say the machinery produces machine tools rather than military instruments.

subfiles.title: Confidential transmittal to the American ambassador in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards Hornbeck’s memorandum on the proposed Wooster plant transfer.
subfiles.summary: Encloses the February 6 conversation memorandum for strictly confidential information.

subfiles.title: McKee’s note forwarding plant information
subfiles.about: Forwards information considered relevant to the plant transfer.
subfiles.summary: McKee sends a memorandum and associated clipping to Messersmith.

subfiles.title: Note on United Engineering’s Wooster plant
subfiles.about: Reports a plan to send a purchased rolling mill equipment plant to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Says United Engineering bought the idle Wooster plant and would join Japanese partners to make steel machinery.

subfiles.title: Pittsburgh Press newspaper clippings
subfiles.from: Raymond Clapper; Drew Pearson and Robert S. Allen
subfiles.about: Discusses U.S. neutrality politics and alleged Nazi propaganda activity.
subfiles.summary: Clapper describes Republican attacks on Roosevelt’s foreign policy and debate over neutrality. A second column reports alleged Nazi Bund propaganda instructions and includes political anecdotes. Page 62 repeats much of the first clipping; page 63 continues the second column.

subfiles.title: Messersmith’s acknowledgment to McKee
subfiles.about: Acknowledges McKee’s memorandum and newspaper clipping.
subfiles.summary: Messersmith thanks McKee for forwarding material of interest.

subfiles.title: Memorandum for Colonel Churchill
subfiles.about: Transmits information on an alleged American and Japanese steel machinery venture.
subfiles.summary: Forwards the information and notes that it is also going to naval intelligence.

subfiles.title: Memorandum for Commander Nixon
subfiles.about: Transmits information on the alleged steel machinery venture.
subfiles.summary: Forwards the information and notes that it is also going to military intelligence.

subfiles.title: Senator Donahey’s inquiry about American branch plants abroad
subfiles.about: Asks about the Wooster transfer and the prevalence of American branch plants overseas.
subfiles.summary: Donahey forwards a worker’s letter and requests statistics on American factories established abroad.

subfiles.title: R. B. Logsdon’s letter on the Wooster plant
subfiles.about: Protests the planned move of the Wooster factory to Japan and discusses unemployment benefits.
subfiles.summary: Logsdon, a machinist at the plant, says its removal would cost about 150 jobs and could put American machinery to Japanese use. He is particularly concerned for older workers. He also opposes a proposed Ohio change to the calculation of unemployment benefits for workers on reduced hours.

subfiles.title: Hull’s reply to Senator Donahey
subfiles.about: Refers Donahey’s request for branch factory data to the Commerce Department.
subfiles.summary: Hull says Commerce has studied foreign branch factories and returns Logsdon’s letter.

subfiles.title: Referral to the Secretary of Commerce
subfiles.about: Forwards Donahey’s and Logsdon’s letters for consideration.
subfiles.summary: Requests Commerce’s consideration of the proposed Wooster plant transfer and Donahey’s inquiry.

subfiles.title: Internal memorandum on the Wooster machine shop reports
subfiles.about: Reviews press reports and recommends against making an issue of the plant transfer.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum links two press reports to Hornbeck’s February conversation with the businessmen. It reasons that further persuasion is unlikely to reverse an apparently completed agreement and recommends no immediate public statement on discouraging credits to Japan.

subfiles.title: Wooster Plant Moves to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports United Engineering’s plan to move its Wooster machine shop to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Company president George T. Ladd says dismantling will begin soon; the plant employs about 150–200 workers.

subfiles.title: U.S. Plant Plans Removal to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports the planned abandonment of the Wooster plant and transfer of machinery to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Walter Locker attributes the company’s consolidation to taxes and operating costs.

subfiles.title: Possible Supplying of Steel Products to Japan on Credit
subfiles.about: Records a discussion with George W. Wolfe and Robert M. Field about steel sales to Japan on credit.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck explains that U.S. law does not forbid steel sales or related credits to Japan, but the Department discourages credit because of Japanese actions in China. He disputes the assumption that Japan will permanently control Chinese ports and suggests China may be the stronger long-term market. The discussion ends with his criticism of Graeme Howard’s recent speech.
